title: Bengio tells lab safety staff to quit — exit as the last lever
summary: Yoshua Bengio's open letter urging safety-minded researchers to leave the frontier labs, and whether an organized exit could do what resignations and regulation haven't. Then how Asana's StackAI made a browser agent 76x cheaper, mostly by fixing a cache it kept breaking, and the week in review.

topics: Yoshua Bengio's open letter in Transformer (8 October 2026) urging frontier-lab staff who prioritize safety to leave for AI Safety Institutes, mission-driven organizations or LawZero: his admitted motivated reasoning; UN Security Council briefing and the 1946 Baruch Plan; Altman and Amodei giving similar speeches ('We have a choice in front of us' — 'Sam's exact words') versus actions; no faith in timely regulation; Jacob Coxon's Time quote on 'almost resignation' inside Anthropic; LawZero's >$200M from Canada and Germany; 'No one of us can stop the race, but enough of us can.' Framed with Hirschman's exit/voice; Alan's selection-effect and reference-class objections (every lab was founded on the same premise)

Asana StackAI browser agent cost study (Frank Hidalgo, 8 October 2026): cache reads 0.05-0.1x input price; cache reuses only the longest unchanged prefix, and per-step screenshot removal plus history trimming broke reuse almost every call; fix = cache the history plus 20:1 batch pruning and a 480k-character budget; 144+12 runs, four models; 76x cheaper/5x faster on GPT-6.1 Sol (89% input from cache) versus original Model B baseline, 29x/4x like-for-like on Model B; caching without batch pruning cost more on three of four models; GPT-6 Astra in Codex ran the investigation in about a week

dives.story: Bengio's case for leaving the labs
dives.why_it_matters: Frontier-lab researchers and policy watchers: the most-cited AI researcher is explicitly organizing talent exit as leverage on the labs, after a run of safety departures and firings.

dives.story: A seventy-six times cheaper agent, mostly from a cache
dives.why_it_matters: Anyone running long agent sessions: Asana's controlled runs show history-management choices that break prompt-cache prefixes can swing cost by more than an order of magnitude on the same model.

concepts_taught: prompt-cache prefix matching in agent loops: caches reuse only the longest unchanged prefix, so per-step pruning of history breaks reuse, batch pruning (e.g. 20:1) preserves it, and caching without matching pruning can cost more than not caching

lore.note: Alan checked his own logging proxy after the Asana study and found his home harness drops old tool output every turn to keep context tidy, so his cache-read share is 'embarrassing' — he has been paying full price to be neat.
